prayer.text: Saint Faustina Kowalska, pray for us.

cues.text: A Peasant Girl's Vocation
Born Helena Kowalska in 1905 to a poor farming family in Głogowiec, Poland, she was one of ten children.
She felt drawn to religious life from as young as age seven but was refused permission by her parents.
Instead, she was forced to work as a housekeeper as a teenager to help support her family.
She never received more than three semesters of formal schooling.
A Vision That Changed Her Path
At nineteen, while attending a dance with her sister, Helena reported a vision of the suffering Christ.
It so moved her that she left the gathering immediately, went to a nearby church, and understood herself instructed to go to Warsaw and enter religious life without delay.
She entered the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in 1925, taking the name Sister Maria Faustina .
Ordinary Work, Extraordinary Visions
Within her convent, Faustina held humble, largely unremarkable positions, serving as cook, gardener, and doorkeeper across several of the congregation's houses.
Even as she held these positions, she reported an ongoing series of visions and conversations with Christ concerning his boundless mercy toward sinners.
He told her to record this message faithfully for the wider Church.
The Divine Mercy Image and Devotion
Under the guidance of her confessor, Fr. Michał Sopoćko, Faustina commissioned an artist to paint an image of Christ as she had seen him.
It showed pale and red rays streaming from his heart, with the inscription 'Jesus, I trust in You' — the now-familiar Divine Mercy image.
She also recorded instructions for a Chaplet of the Divine Mercy and requested, on Christ's behalf as she reported it, that a feast of the Divine Mercy be established on the Sunday after Easter.
A Hidden Diary
At her superiors' direction, Faustina kept a detailed diary of her visions and mystical experiences from 1934 onward, eventually filling six notebooks.
The text was known only to her spiritual director during her lifetime, but published after her death as Divine Mercy in My Soul .
Since then, it has become one of the most widely read spiritual texts of the modern era.
Legacy
Faustina's health, always fragile, declined steadily through the 1930s, and she died of tuberculosis at Kraków in 1938 at only thirty-three.
Faustina was canonized in 2000 by Pope John Paul II , himself a fellow Pole with a lifelong devotion to her message.
At her canonization the pope declared the Sunday after Easter 'Divine Mercy Sunday' for the universal Church.
This formally established the very feast Faustina had reported Christ requesting more than sixty years earlier.
